intro: Olive oil in coffee has been showing up online as a trend, usually with a spoon stirred into the cup and a claim attached about energy or metabolism.
This article skips the claims: how much oil to use, why it needs blending or vigorous stirring rather than a plain pour, what it tastes like, which grade suits it, and hot versus iced.

sections.heading: A texture trend, not a health trend

blocks.text: Most of what circulates about olive oil coffee online is framed as a metabolism boost or a healthier latte. This article does not make that case: it treats the drink as what it is on the palate, a fuller mouthfeel and a flavour note, nothing about disease or energy.
If the real question is whether it is good for you, that is one for a doctor or dietitian, not a recipe article. What follows is only how it's made and what it tastes like.

sections.heading: How much oil, and how to mix it in

blocks.text: Start with roughly half a teaspoon of extra virgin olive oil per cup — a small amount, since the point is a texture change, not an oily drink. Oil and coffee do not mix on their own, so a plain pour just sits as a slick on top.

items: Brew the coffee as usual, hot or over ice.
Measure roughly half a teaspoon of a mild extra virgin olive oil.
Add the oil to the cup, then stir hard and continuously for ten to fifteen seconds, or blend for a few seconds in a small frother or blender.
Taste, and add a few more drops only if the mouthfeel still feels thin.
Drink promptly — left standing, the oil separates back out and beads on the surface.

blocks.text: Done right, the coffee feels fuller and slightly heavier on the tongue, closer to a drink with a little cream stirred through than a black coffee. It is not sweet, and it does not taste of olives in any strong way if the oil is mild.

The main effect is on bitterness: a faint, grassy note sits underneath the coffee and takes the edge off a sharp cup rather than masking the coffee flavour. Too much oil tips it the other way and the drink turns greasy.

sections.heading: Which oil suits coffee, and which doesn't

blocks.text: A mild extra virgin olive oil works better here than a peppery, high-intensity one, which fights the coffee instead of rounding it out. Arabian Village's plain extra virgin, poured in small quantity, keeps the coffee flavour in front rather than competing with it.
None of the six infused oils belong in a cup of coffee — they're built for savoury dishes, not a drink. See [the products page](/products) for the plain oil and its two sizes.

Hot coffee mixes the oil in faster because heat thins it, so a firm stir for ten seconds is usually enough. Cold or iced coffee needs more work — the oil stays thicker and separates back out sooner, so a blender or milk frother does a more even job than a spoon.

sections.heading: Where this fits next to your other coffee habits

blocks.text: This is a one-cup experiment, not a routine to build a diet around, and it sits alongside milk, sugar or a plain black coffee rather than replacing any of them. If it isn't for you, nothing is lost by leaving the oil out.

For the same oil in savoury cooking rather than a cup, [how to cook with olive oil in a Malaysian kitchen](/blog/how-to-cook-with-olive-oil-in-a-malaysian-kitchen) covers pan heat, seasoning and everyday dishes.

Olive oil coffee is a texture experiment: about half a teaspoon of a mild extra virgin oil, mixed in hard rather than poured, gives a fuller mouthfeel and softens bitterness. It is worth trying once out of curiosity, not as a health routine — leave the disease and energy claims to a dietitian.

faqs.q: Is olive oil coffee good for you?
faqs.a: That is a question for a doctor or dietitian, not a recipe article. This piece only covers what the drink tastes like and how to make it — a fuller mouthfeel and a softened bitterness, nothing more.

faqs.q: How much olive oil should I put in coffee?
faqs.a: Start with about half a teaspoon per cup. It is a small amount because the goal is a texture change, not an oily drink — add a few more drops only if it still tastes thin.

faqs.q: Why does the oil float on top of my coffee?
faqs.a: Oil and coffee don't mix on their own, so a plain pour sits as a slick. Stir hard for ten to fifteen seconds, or blend briefly, so the oil breaks up through the drink instead of pooling.

faqs.q: Which olive oil is best for coffee?
faqs.a: A mild extra virgin oil works better than a peppery, high-intensity one, which fights the coffee's own flavour. None of the infused flavours suit a cup — they're built for savoury cooking, not a drink.

faqs.q: Can I add olive oil to iced coffee?
faqs.a: Yes, though it takes more work than hot coffee — cold oil separates back out faster. A small blender or milk frother mixes it more evenly than stirring with a spoon.

faqs.q: What does olive oil coffee actually taste like?
faqs.a: Fuller and slightly heavier on the tongue, closer to coffee with a little cream than black coffee. It isn't sweet, and with a mild oil it doesn't taste strongly of olives.

faqs.q: Does olive oil coffee replace milk or sugar?
faqs.a: No — it sits alongside them, not as a replacement. Some people add oil to plain black coffee, others still add milk or sugar as usual; there's no fixed rule.
